Days with a complete entry were 91 percent with the electronic diary and 64 percent with paper. Counts of headache days agreed closely when both were complete, but paper diaries were often filled in retrospectively just before appointments. Participants aged over 65 preferred paper more often. The study did not examine treatment decisions or appointment use."},{"title":"Headache diaries and eligibility for injectable preventive treatment in specialist clinics","authors":"Halvorsen-Osei M, Duarte-Frost L","year":2021,"venue":"Clinical Headache Practice","doi":"10.5555/chp.2021.0206","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 620 consecutive appointments in four specialist headache clinics where eligibility for injectable preventive treatment was being considered. In all, 31 percent of patients arrived without a usable diary. Among them, the eligibility decision was deferred to a further appointment in 58 percent. Deferred decisions added a median of 11 weeks before treatment started. Clinics that sent a diary reminder before the appointment had fewer unusable diaries. The review did not record why diaries were missing or incomplete, and clinics differed in how they defined a usable diary."},{"title":"Appointment length and diary availability in a hospital headache clinic","authors":"Mwangi-Holloway P, Sato-Brennan K","year":2023,"venue":"Neurology Services Research","doi":"10.5555/nsr.2023.0058","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We timed 410 follow-up appointments in a hospital headache clinic. Appointments without a usable diary were 6 minutes longer on average than appointments with one, mostly spent reconstructing headache frequency from memory. Clinicians rated their confidence in treatment decisions lower when no diary was available. The clinic's booked slot length did not change, so longer appointments delayed later patients in the session. The study was done in a single clinic over three months, and the clinicians knew their appointments were being timed."},{"title":"Older adults and smartphone health apps in neurology outpatients: use and barriers","authors":"Ferreira-Lindqvist E, Adeyemi-Wong J","year":2016,"venue":"Journal of Digital Neurology","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 530 neurology outpatients about smartphone use and health apps. Among patients aged 70 or over, 44 percent did not own a smartphone and a further 21 percent owned one but had never installed an app. Barriers included small screens, sight problems and worry about data sharing. Younger patients used health apps widely. The authors recommend that any switch to app-based monitoring keeps a paper option and offers help with setting up. The survey was done in one hospital and may not reflect rural services."},{"title":"Budget impact of expanding access to injectable migraine preventives in a regional health service","authors":"Nakagawa-Pryce D, Oduya-Stein H","year":2024,"venue":"Neurology Health Economics","doi":"10.5555/nhe.2024.0031","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We estimated the three-year budget impact of injectable migraine preventives for a regional health service. Each additional treated patient cost 4,900 per year in drug costs in local currency. Better documentation of headache days was projected to raise the number of eligible patients by 18 percent, and the budget impact was driven almost entirely by drug costs rather than clinic time. The estimate did not include savings from fewer emergency visits. Uptake assumptions came from a single year of local prescribing data."},{"title":"Nurse time needed to set up digital symptom apps for outpatients","authors":"Brandt-Mensah A, Kowalski-Tanaka F","year":2020,"venue":"Outpatient Nursing Practice","doi":"10.5555/onp.2020.0147","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We timed nurse-led set-up sessions for a digital symptom app in three outpatient clinics. The median set-up time was 14 minutes per patient, and 22 percent of patients needed a second session. Set-up took longest for patients aged over 75 and for those who needed an interpreter. After set-up, most patients kept using the app for at least three months. Nurse time was not replaced by any reduction in other clinic tasks. The study did not compare app set-up with the time needed to explain a paper diary."},{"title":"Headache diary standards for specialist clinics: consensus recommendations","authors":"Specialist Headache Nurses Network","year":null,"venue":"Consensus statement series","providerType":"guideline","abstract":"A panel of headache nurses and neurologists agreed minimum standards for headache diaries used in specialist clinics. A usable diary should cover at least 28 consecutive days, record headache days and acute medication days, and be completed prospectively. The panel recommends that clinics offer both paper and electronic diaries and check usability before the appointment. The statement gives no publication date and describes its consensus process only briefly. It suggests that clinics audit the share of patients arriving with a usable diary at least once a year."}]}
